Autoantibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (Gad-Abs) are implicated in various neurological syndromes. The
present study aims to identify intrathecal-speci ﬁc GAD-Abs and to determine clinical manifestations and
treatment outcomes. Nineteen patients had GAD-Abs in cerebrospinal ﬂuid but not in paired serum samples.
Neurological syndromes included limbic encephalitis, temporal lobe epilepsy, cerebellar ataxia, autonomic
dysfunction, and stiff-person syndrome. Immunotherapy had bene ﬁcial effects in 57.1% of patients, and the
patients with limbic encephalitis responded especially well to immunotherapy. Intrathecal-speciﬁca n t i b o d i e s
to GAD at low titers may appear as nonspeciﬁc markers of immune activation within the central nervous system
rather than pathogenic antibodies causing neuronal dysfunction.

1. Introduction
Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) is an enzyme that catalyzes the
transformation of glutamate intoγ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), which is
the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system
(CNS). Autoantibodies to GAD (GAD-Abs) were documented to involve
a variety of neurological syndromes such as stiff-person syndrome,
cerebellar ataxia, limbic encephalitis, and epilepsy ( Dalakas et al.,
2000; Honnorat et al., 2001; Liimatainen et al., 2010; Malter et al.,
2010). However, the pathogenicity of GAD-Abs with respect to neuro-
logical syndromes has been questioned, mainly because of the intracel-
lular location of GAD in the CNS. A recent study investigating the
pathogenicity of GAD-Abs in stiff-person syndromes suggested that
there were coexisting antibodies within the serum that bound to the
surface of GABAergic neurons and that might be pathogenic ( Chang
et al., 2013). However, the beneﬁcial effects of immunotherapy as well
as the passive transfer of IgG from patients with GAD-Abs to affect
neuronal excitability both supported that GAD-Abs were involved in the
pathogenesis or were at least possible markers of the autoimmune-
mediated process in neurological syndromes ( Dalakas et al., 2001a;
Manto et al., 2007).
Over the past few years, the authors have investigated patients who
were presumed to have immune-mediated neurological diseases,

including those of paraneoplastic and non-paraneoplastic origins
(Kim et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2014; Moon et al., 2014; Shin et al., 2013 ).
Upon evaluating the presence of neuronal autoantibodies from paired
serum and cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) samples, we occasionally found
that the CSF samples were positive but serum samples were negative
for GAD-Abs. However, most of the previous studies focused on high
serum titers of GAD-Abs in association with neurological syndromes
(Arino et al., 2014; Malter et al., 2010; Saiz et al., 2008 ). Although the
diagnostic value of low-titer antibodies to GAD65 remained less clear,
growing evidence suggested that patients with low antibody titers
could be associated with GAD autoimmunity ( Errichiello et al., 2009;
Liimatainen et al., 2010; Meinck et al., 2001; Nanri et al., 2013 ).
Nevertheless, to the best of our knowledge, GAD-Abs limited to CSF in
neurological syndromes have not been documented in the literature.

The aim of the present study is to investigate intrathecal-speci ﬁc
GAD-Abs in patients with presumed autoimmune neurological diseases
and to describe the clinical characteristics, laboratory ﬁndings, and
treatment outcomes.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Patients
This study was approved by the institutional review board of Seoul
National University Hospital. GAD-Abs and other neuronal autoanti-
bodies were tested in serum and CSF when patients were suspected to
have autoimmune neurological syndromes, most of which included
limbic encephalitis, focal epilepsy of recent onset, autonomic dysfunc-
tion, cerebellar ataxia, stiff-person syndrome, and progressive encepha-
lomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM). We selected patients
whose CSF tested positive for GAD-Abs from June 2012 to September
2014. Among these patients, we excluded those whose serum revealed
increased GAD-Ab levels. Although this limited the number of subjects
eligible for the study, it enabled us to focus on the clinical implications
of intrathecal-speciﬁc GAD autoimmunity. All patients were admitted
to Seoul National University Hospital and examined by the authors.
We investigated detailed neurologic features and the functional status,
measured by the modiﬁed Rankin scale (mRS). The clinical syndromes
of the patients were determined based upon the predominant neuro-
logic symptoms and signs and the absence of another diagnosis that
could explain the clinical presentation. The main syndromes comprised
stiff-person syndrome, cerebellar ataxia, limbic encephalitis, and epilep-
sy; otherwise unclassi ﬁed cases were included in the others group.
We performed a series of investigations, including neuroimaging, CSF
analysis, electroencephalography (EEG), and tumor screening tests.
Clinical improvement was de ﬁned as a decrease of the mRS score by
at least one point at the last visit compared with the initial mRS score.
The authors obtained written informed consent from all patients or
their representatives.
2.2. Detection of GAD-Abs
GAD-Ab levels were measured by radioimmunoassay (RIA) accord-
ing to the manufacturer's protocol (RSR Limited, U.K.) in the diagnostic
laboratory, department of nuclear medicine, Seoul National University.
Brieﬂy, 20 μL of each patient's serum and CSF samples, calibrators
(0–300 U/mL), and controls were mixed with 50 μLo f
125I-labeled
GAD65. After incubation for 2 h, 50μL of protein A was added to precip-
itate labeled GAD antigen-antibody complexes. After a further one-hour
incubation period, 1 mL of assay buffer was added and centrifuged at
1500× g for 30 min at 4 °C. Any unbound125I was removed by aspiration
of the supernatants, and the pellets were counted on a gamma counter.
The GAD-Ab levels in patient samples were then read off from the cali-
bration curve constructed by plotting the calibrator concentration
against the percentage of binding. The lower detection limit of the
assay is 0.1 U/mL. Serum or CSF titers N 1.0 U/mL were considered posi-
tive, and positive samples were tested again for conﬁrmation. This assay
showed 95% speciﬁcity and 84% sensitivity for diagnosing type I diabe-
tes in the 2005 Diabetes Antibody Standardization Program (DASP).
2.3. Assay for other neural autoantibodies
Screening tests for neural autoantibodies were performed as previously
described (Kim et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2014; Moon et al., 2014; Shin et al.,
2013). Antigenic targets of the assay included neuronal surface proteins

(N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR),α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-meth-
yl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR), voltage-gated potassium
channel (VGKC)-complex containing leucine-rich glioma inactivated 1
(LGI1) and contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2),γ-aminobutyric
acid receptor-B (GABA
B)) and classic paraneoplastic antigens (Hu, Yo, Ri,
CV2/CRMP5, Ma2, amphiphysin). To detect antibodies against neuronal
surface proteins, cell-based indirect immuno ﬂuorescence tests were
employed following the manufacturer's instructions (Euroimmun,
Germany). Classic paraneoplastic antibodies were detected by immuno-
blotting (Euroimmun, Germany).
2.4. Statistical analysis
Signiﬁcant differences between two groups were assessed using the
Mann–Whitney U test or Fisher's exact test based on the nature of the
variables. The Kruskal–Wallis test was used to compare non-categorical
variables such as antibody titers and mRS scores of more than two
groups. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was employed to compare mRS
scores before and after immunotherapy. Spearman's rho ( ρ) was used
to measure the correlation between two variables. SPSS 21 was used
for all statistical analysis, and a two-tailed P value less than 0.05 was
considered signiﬁcant.
3. Results
3.1. Clinical features of patients with intrathecal GAD-Abs
A total of 32 patients were screened for the presence of GAD-Abs in
serum and CSF. The initial diagnosis was limbic encephalitis in nine
patients, autonomic dysfunction in seven, localization-related epilepsy
in six, cerebellar ataxia in four, stiff-person syndrome in three, PERM
in one, Meige syndrome in one, and brainstem encephalitis in one.
Among them, four patientsﬁnally received a different diagnosis: proba-
ble Creutzfeldt –Jakob disease (CJD) in three patients and vestibular
schwannoma in one. Further nine patients were excluded because
GAD-Ab titers were also increased in the paired serum samples
(Supplementary Table 1). Finally, the remaining 19 patients (59.4%)
tested positive for GAD-Abs in CSF but not in serum samples. Demo-
graphic and clinical information is shown in Table 1. The median age
at detection of GAD-Abs was 46 years (range, 16 –77), and twelve of
the patients were female (63.2%). The median time from symptom
onset to diagnosis was 9 months (range, 0.2 –82). The median titer of
GAD-Abs in CSF was 3.51 U/mL (range, 2.25 –5.86). GAD-Abs were not
detected in paired serum samples in 16 patients (below 0.1 U/mL). In
the other three patients, serum GAD-Ab titers fell within the normal
limits, ranging between 0.23 and 0.35 U/mL. No patients had received
any immunotherapy before the antibody evaluation. In general, CSF
GAD-Ab titers were not correlated with the duration of neurologic
symptoms (ρ =0 . 0 7 8 ,P = 0.648) or initial mRS scores ( ρ = − 0.018,
P = 0.943). In terms of past medical history, no patient had type 1
diabetes mellitus (DM), but two patients had type 2 DM. None of the pa-
tients had a clinical history with other autoimmune diseases. Regarding
tumor history, one patient had breast cancer, which was successfully
treated 18 months prior and was in remission at the time of this
presentation.

3.2. Neurological manifestations
There were a variety of neurological syndromes associated
with GAD-Abs. The most common syndrome was limbic encephalitis,
which was present in six patients (31.6%). They showed typical features
comprising acute or subacute cognitive dysfunction, seizures, and psychi-
atric symptoms. Four patients presented with isolated epilepsy, three
with cerebellar ataxia, and one with stiff-person syndrome. The neuro-
logical syndromes of the otherﬁve patients included dizziness, diplopia,
and Meige syndrome. Among them, dizziness was present in four pa-
tients, diplopia in one, and Meige syndrome in one (Supplementary
Table 1). CSF GAD-Ab titers did not differ among the clinical presentation
subgroups (P =0 . 8 1 3 ,Fig. 1A). However, the degree of disability at diag-
nosis varied with the clinical syndromes (P = 0.022, Fig. 1B); initial mRS
scores of stiff-person syndrome, cerebellar ataxia and limbic encephalitis
groups were higher than those of epilepsy and others (median, 3 vs 1,P b
0.01).
The most common clinical features were seizures, which affected ten
patients (52.6%): complex partial seizures in seven, secondarily general-
ized tonic clonic seizures in six, and simple partial seizures and status
epilepticus in one patient, respectively. According to the semiologic fea-
tures and EEG ﬁndings, seizures were classi ﬁed as being of temporal
lobe origin in eight patients, parietal lobe origin in one, and unclear
localization in one. In addition to the four patients with isolated epilep-
sy, seizures occurred in ﬁve patients with limbic encephalitis and one
patient with stiff-person syndrome. Cognitive dysfunction was the
second most common symptom and presented in six patients (31.6%).
Four patients (21.1%) had psychiatric symptoms, including agitation,
aggressive behavior, anxiety, and depression. Especially in the two
cases of limbic encephalitis, psychotic features with hallucination, disor-
ganized behavior, and hyperactivity were the major concerns. Basal
ganglia involvement was evident in two patients: oromandibular dyski-
nesia and dystonia of the limbs were observed in a patient with limbic
encephalitis, and blepharospasm, jaw deviation, and dystonia involving
the face and neck were observed in a patient initially diagnosed with
Meige syndrome. Cerebellar dysfunction with gait ataxia and prominent
limb dysmetria was documented in three patients; two of them also
demonstrated dysarthria and gaze-evoked nystagmus. Thoracic and
abdominal CT and whole body 18- ﬂuorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-PET
scans to exclude a paraneoplastic cause were all negative. Genetic
tests for spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) types 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 19 and
dentatorubral–pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA) were performed in two
patients and revealed no genetic abnormalities. Hyperreﬂexia was pres-
ent in two patients, one with stiff-person syndrome and the other with
cerebellar ataxia. Autonomic dysfunction was reported in four patients,
orthostatic hypotension in two and postural orthostatic tachycardia
syndrome in two patients. Dizziness and insomnia were also noted.

3.3. Investigations
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans were available in all
patients, and signiﬁcant abnormalities were detected in four patients;
temporal lobe involvement was found in two patients, marked cerebel-
lar atrophy was found in one, and diffuse cortical lesion was found in

one (Fig. 2A–D). Brain FDG-PET scans were performed in nine patients,
and four showed abnormal hypometabolism ( Fig. 2E–I); two of them
had corresponding structural lesions in the brain MRI ( Fig. 2 E, F).
Hypermetabolic abnormalities were not found in any patients.
Tumor screening tests were carried out in sixteen patients. Whole-
body FDG-PET scans failed to reveal abnormal hypermetabolism. Chest
and abdomen CT identi ﬁed three patients with a benign tumor; a
benign ovarian cyst was found in twopatients, and focal nodular hyper-
plasia of the liver was found in one. Malignant tumors were not detected.
All patients underwent serologic evaluation for detecting neural au-
toantibodies. Although antibodies to neural surface proteins were not
detected in any patients, paraneoplastic antibodies were positive in
three patients. Two patients presenting with Meige syndrome and diz-
ziness, respectively, tested positive for anti-Yo antibodies, but there
was no clinical evidence of cerebellar degeneration. One patient with
epilepsy was positive for Ma2 antibodies. All patients tested negative
for malignancy. Other coexisting autoantibodies were found in two
patients; one patient had euthyroid anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO) anti-
bodies, and the other had antinuclear antibodies without clinical evi-
dence of systemic autoimmune diseases. The results of neuroimaging,
laboratory and electrophysiological tests are summarized inTable 3.

and the median time from the disease onset to the beginning of treat-

In general, patients with improvement had shorter disease durations

cerebellar ataxia showed no improvement after immunotherapy and
failed to show a decrease of antibody levels. The serial CSF GAD-Ab titers
and mRS scores in association with immunotherapy of these two cases

4. Discussion
Here, we identiﬁed nineteen patients who had low-titer GAD-Abs in
CSF but not in paired serum samples and described the clinical features,
investigation results and treatment outcomes. Intrathecal-speci ﬁc
GAD-Abs were associated with various neurological syndromes such
as limbic encephalitis, localization-related epilepsy, cerebellar ataxia,
autonomic dysfunction and stiff-person syndrome. There was no clear
evidence of other organ-speci ﬁc autoimmunity such as type 1 DM or
thyroiditis, although one patient tested positive for anti-TPO Abs with-
out thyroid dysfunction. Malignant tumors were not evident. In general,
immunotherapy resulted in favorable outcomes; eight (57.1%) out of
fourteen patients showed clinical improvement, whereas none of
the four patients who did not receive immunotherapy experienced
any improvement. In particular, all patients with limbic encephalitis
responded to immunotherapy. Clinical improvement was related to
the short disease duration.
The main ﬁnding of the present study was the identi ﬁcation of
CSF-speciﬁc GAD-Abs in patients presumed to have autoimmune neu-
rological diseases. The exclusive presence of GAD-Abs in CSF indicated
intrathecal antibody synthesis by B cells, which were recruited and
activated within the CNS ( Irani et al., 2014; Vincent et al., 2011 ). This
result was consistent with those of other studies demonstrating that
GAD-Ab-producing B cell clones were present within the CNS of
patients with stiff-person syndrome (Jarius et al., 2010; Skorstad et al.,
2008). Furthermore, the intrathecal production of GAD-speci ﬁc
antibodies was described in previous studies that demonstrated elevat-
ed GAD-Ab indices in the majority of patients with various GAD-
associated neurological syndromes ( Arino et al., 2014; Dalakas et al.,
2001b; Malter et al., 2010 ). Given that neurological manifestations
with high serum titers of GAD-Abs were frequently accompanied by
polyendocrine autoimmunity ( Costa et al., 2002 ), the absence of
coexisting autoimmune diseases in our subjects also corresponded to
humoral immunity limited to the CNS. In addition to GAD-Abs,

intrathecal antibody synthesis was frequently observed in patients with
neuroglial surface-directed antibodies such as NMDAR, AMPAR,
GABABR, and glycine receptor antibodies (Irani et al., 2014). Regarding
the sensitivity of antibody testing, 13.2% of patients with NMDAR en-
cephalitis did not reveal serum antibodies by the time of diagnosis,
whereas CSF antibodies were positive in all patients ( Gresa-Arribas
et al., 2014).
On the other hand, the clinical signi ﬁcance of intrathecal-speci ﬁc
GAD-Abs is limited for several reasons. First, intrathecal antibody
synthesis itself does not con ﬁrm the pathogenic role of the antibody
(Vincent, 2008), although it may suggest that the primary disease pro-
cess occurs within the CNS (Malter et al., 2013). Furthermore, intrathe-
cal antibody production without serum antibodies is uncommon in
autoantibody-mediated neurological disorders. Second, CSF titers of
the antibodies are too low compared with those of previous reports
demonstrating typical GAD-Ab-associated neurological syndromes
with high serum titers ( Malter et al., 2010; Rakocevic et al., 2004 ).
Lack of correlation between CSF GAD-Ab titers and disease severity
also support the notion that the low-titer antibodies are not directly in-
volved in the CNS dysfunction. Finally, the spectrum of neurological
syndromes is quite broad in this study. Some patients presented with
autonomic dysfunction or oromandibular dyskinesia, but its association
with GAD autoimmunity is not well established. Moreover, CSF
GAD-Abs were also positive in the patients ﬁnally diagnosed with
non-autoimmune neurological disorders, such as CJD and vestibular
schwannoma. In this regard, intrathecal GAD-Abs cannot be used as a
diagnostic marker for GAD Ab-associated neurological diseases. It is
similar to intrathecal oligoclonal bands which are nonspeciﬁcm a r k e r s
of immune activation within the CNS and found in a wide range of neu-
rological disorders such as demyelinating diseases, other autoimmune-
mediated diseases, and infectious encephalitis ( Petzold, 2013). Taken
together, it is presumed that intrathecal GAD-Abs at low titers appear
as nonspeci ﬁc ﬁndings of CNS in ﬂammation rather than pathogenic
antibodies directly leading to neuronal dysfunction.
In terms of neurological syndromes, non-paraneoplastic limbic
encephalitis was the most common (31.6%) presentation. Limbic
encephalitis has been reported to be associated with GAD-Abs ( Blanc
et al., 2009; Malter et al., 2010; Markakis et al., 2014; Mata et al.,
2008). In particular, our data suggested that limbic encephalitis associ-
ated with intrathecal GAD-Abs was responsive to immunotherapy as
all patients achieved functional improvement after immunotherapy.
Previous studies also showed a favorable response to immunotherapy
with a parallel decrease in GAD-Ab titers ( Blanc et al., 2009; Markakis
et al., 2014). In contrast, a series of nine patients with GAD-associated
limbic encephalitis demonstrated inferior outcomes in seizure control
and memory function after corticosteroid therapy compared with
VGKC-Ab-positive patients ( Malter et al., 2010 ). Taken together with
the modest reduction in antibody titers, the unfavorable outcomes im-
plied that high-dose corticosteroids alone might be insufﬁcient for the
treatment of GAD-Ab-associated limbic encephalitis and that additional
immunotherapy might be required to more ef ﬁciently eliminate the

circulating antibodies. In agreement with this, all patients with limbic
encephalitis in our series received repeated rituximab infusions as the
2nd line immunotherapy before clinical improvement occurred.
Isolated epilepsy of temporal lobe origin was the second most
common syndrome (21.1%). Epilepsy was also present in patients
with limbic encephalitis or stiff-person syndrome, and most of them
had temporal lobe seizures. It has been increasingly accepted that
autoimmune mechanisms contributed in part to epilepsy even in the
absence of limbic encephalitis phenotypes, and GAD-Ab was one of
the best-known antibodies in immune-mediated epilepsy ( McKnight
et al., 2005; Quek et al., 2012 ). Previous data demonstrated that 3.9%
to 5.4% of patients with drug-resistant epilepsy had high serum titers
of GAD-Abs (
Lilleker et al., 2014; Peltola et al., 2000 ), and consistent
with our ﬁndings, most of the patients had temporal lobe epilepsy
(Errichiello et al., 2009; Falip et al., 2012; Liimatainen et al., 2010 ).
Although there were con ﬂicting results regarding immunotherapy
responses, the successful treatment of refractory epilepsy after immu-
notherapy has been reported in previous cases ( Farooqi et al., 2015;
Kanter et al., 2008 ). Furthermore, cortical GABA levels were reported
to decrease in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy and GAD-Abs,
but there was no difference in a composite measure of glutamate and
glutamine (Stagg et al., 2010). These ﬁndings supported the pathogenic
role of GAD-Abs in epilepsy, although the exact mechanism of GAD
autoimmunity has not been fully understood.
Cerebellar ataxia is a well-recognized neurological syndrome associ-
ated with GAD-Abs especially of high serum titers ( Honnorat et al.,
2001; Saiz et al., 2008 ). (Nanri et al., 2013 ) In our data, three patients
(15.8%) presented with subacute or chronic cerebellar ataxia, and
cerebellar dysfunction was corroborated by the brain imaging which
revealed marked cerebellar atrophy in one patient and cerebellar
hypometabolism in two. One patient who responded to immunothera-
py had relatively short disease duration (4 months) before therapy and
decreased glucose metabolism without apparent cerebellar atrophy.
These ﬁndings indicate that early immunotherapy might provide favor-
able outcomes in cerebellar ataxia associated with GAD-Abs, which is
consistent with previous study favoring the prompt immunotherapy
(Arino et al., 2014).
Notably, four patients with otherwise unclassi ﬁed syndromes
presented with isolated dizziness or diplopia. In a recent series of 34
patients with cerebellar ataxia and GAD-Abs, nine (26.5%) patients re-
ported episodes of diplopia or isolated vertigo without other evidence
of cerebellar dysfunction before ataxia was fully developed ( Arino
et al., 2014). These data indicated that subtle and transient symptoms
might herald the development of cerebellar ataxia. A long-term
follow-up study should be performed to con ﬁrm that non-speci ﬁc
symptoms, including dizziness, represent the early phase of GAD
autoimmunity and that earlier immunotherapy can help to prevent or
delay the development of obvious neurologic dysfunction.
In this study, we excluded the patients positive for serum GAD-Abs
from the analysis to focus on intrathecal-speci ﬁc GAD-Abs. Among 32
patients screened, however, 10 patients (31.3%) showed elevated
GAD-Abs in the paired serum samples. While two patients (#11 and

17 in Supplementary Table 1) had high levels (24,000 –84,000 U/mL)
typically shown in GAD Ab-associated neurological syndromes, the
others revealed low-level Abs (1.02 –5.04 U/mL). Diagnostic values of
serum low-titer GAD-Abs have not been established mainly because
elevated GAD-Abs are also common in type 1 DM ( Saiz et al., 1997 ).
However, several studies reported that low-titer GAD-Abs were
implicated in cerebellar ataxia and epilepsy ( Errichiello et al., 2009;
Liimatainen et al., 2010; Nanri et al., 2013 ). Especially, Nanri et al.
(2013) demonstrated effectiveness of immunotherapy in patients
with cerebellar ataxia, providing the potential indications for immuno-
therapy in low-titer GAD-Abs.
Our study has limitations mostly regarding the measurement of
GAD-Abs in CSF. First, we used the commercial RIA kits which were orig-
inally developed for testing serum GAD-Abs. However, our RIA protocol
was not modiﬁed to make the CSF assays equivalent to those for serum,
and the methodological difference consequently might affect the anti-
body titers of CSF samples. Nevertheless, it does not alter the fact that
GAD-Abs are present in CSF tested, although the titers are too low to
emphasize their pathogenic relevance. Second, our ﬁndings were not
conﬁrmed by other methods to measure GAD-Abs. Immunohistochem-
istry is a commonly used method for analysis of GAD-Abs associated
with neurological syndromes, but it can only detect samples with high
GAD-Ab titers ( ≥ 2000 U/mL by RIA) and is not suitable for measure
low-titer antibodies ( Saiz et al., 2008 ). Further research using other
techniques such as immunoblots or cell-based assays will be helpful in
validating the presence of CSF-speciﬁc GAD-Abs. Finally, the study popu-
lation only included patients suspected to have autoimmune neurological
diseases, and lack of healthy controls hinders the understanding of clinical
utility and relevance of intrathecal GAD-Abs. Measuring CSF GAD-Abs in

required to address these questions.
5. Conclusions
Our study showed that intrathecal-speciﬁc antibodies to GAD were
found in patients with various neurological syndromes with a possible
autoimmune basis, such as limbic encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, crypto-
genic focal epilepsy, and stiff-person syndromes. However, measuring
GAD-Abs in CSF could not be used for diagnosis of GAD Ab-associated
neurological disorders because CSF GAD-Abs were also detected in
non-autoimmune neurological diseases. Intrathecal synthesis of
GAD-Abs at low titers may represent nonspeci ﬁc immune activation
and in ﬂammation within the CNS. Further investigations with other
laboratory techniques as well as different disease entities are needed
to con ﬁrm the presence of intrathecal-speci ﬁc GAD-Abs and their
clinical signiﬁcance.

4. Discussion
Here, we identiﬁed nineteen patients who had low-titer GAD-Abs in
CSF but not in paired serum samples and described the clinical features,
investigation results and treatment outcomes. Intrathecal-speci ﬁc
GAD-Abs were associated with various neurological syndromes such
as limbic encephalitis, localization-related epilepsy, cerebellar ataxia,
autonomic dysfunction and stiff-person syndrome. There was no clear
evidence of other organ-speci ﬁc autoimmunity such as type 1 DM or
thyroiditis, although one patient tested positive for anti-TPO Abs with-
out thyroid dysfunction. Malignant tumors were not evident. In general,
immunotherapy resulted in favorable outcomes; eight (57.1%) out of
fourteen patients showed clinical improvement, whereas none of
the four patients who did not receive immunotherapy experienced
any improvement. In particular, all patients with limbic encephalitis
responded to immunotherapy. Clinical improvement was related to
the short disease duration.
The main ﬁnding of the present study was the identi ﬁcation of
CSF-speciﬁc GAD-Abs in patients presumed to have autoimmune neu-
rological diseases. The exclusive presence of GAD-Abs in CSF indicated
intrathecal antibody synthesis by B cells, which were recruited and
activated within the CNS ( Irani et al., 2014; Vincent et al., 2011 ). This
result was consistent with those of other studies demonstrating that
GAD-Ab-producing B cell clones were present within the CNS of
patients with stiff-person syndrome (Jarius et al., 2010; Skorstad et al.,
2008). Furthermore, the intrathecal production of GAD-speci ﬁc
antibodies was described in previous studies that demonstrated elevat-
ed GAD-Ab indices in the majority of patients with various GAD-
associated neurological syndromes ( Arino et al., 2014; Dalakas et al.,
2001b; Malter et al., 2010 ). Given that neurological manifestations
with high serum titers of GAD-Abs were frequently accompanied by
polyendocrine autoimmunity ( Costa et al., 2002 ), the absence of
coexisting autoimmune diseases in our subjects also corresponded to
humoral immunity limited to the CNS. In addition to GAD-Abs,

GABABR, and glycine receptor antibodies (Irani et al., 2014). Regarding
the sensitivity of antibody testing, 13.2% of patients with NMDAR en-
cephalitis did not reveal serum antibodies by the time of diagnosis,
whereas CSF antibodies were positive in all patients ( Gresa-Arribas
et al., 2014).
On the other hand, the clinical signi ﬁcance of intrathecal-speci ﬁc
GAD-Abs is limited for several reasons. First, intrathecal antibody
synthesis itself does not con ﬁrm the pathogenic role of the antibody
(Vincent, 2008), although it may suggest that the primary disease pro-
cess occurs within the CNS (Malter et al., 2013). Furthermore, intrathe-
cal antibody production without serum antibodies is uncommon in
autoantibody-mediated neurological disorders. Second, CSF titers of
the antibodies are too low compared with those of previous reports
demonstrating typical GAD-Ab-associated neurological syndromes
with high serum titers ( Malter et al., 2010; Rakocevic et al., 2004 ).
Lack of correlation between CSF GAD-Ab titers and disease severity
also support the notion that the low-titer antibodies are not directly in-
volved in the CNS dysfunction. Finally, the spectrum of neurological
syndromes is quite broad in this study. Some patients presented with
autonomic dysfunction or oromandibular dyskinesia, but its association
with GAD autoimmunity is not well established. Moreover, CSF
GAD-Abs were also positive in the patients ﬁnally diagnosed with
non-autoimmune neurological disorders, such as CJD and vestibular
schwannoma. In this regard, intrathecal GAD-Abs cannot be used as a
diagnostic marker for GAD Ab-associated neurological diseases. It is
similar to intrathecal oligoclonal bands which are nonspeciﬁcm a r k e r s
of immune activation within the CNS and found in a wide range of neu-
rological disorders such as demyelinating diseases, other autoimmune-
mediated diseases, and infectious encephalitis ( Petzold, 2013). Taken
together, it is presumed that intrathecal GAD-Abs at low titers appear
as nonspeci ﬁc ﬁndings of CNS in ﬂammation rather than pathogenic
antibodies directly leading to neuronal dysfunction.
In terms of neurological syndromes, non-paraneoplastic limbic
encephalitis was the most common (31.6%) presentation. Limbic
encephalitis has been reported to be associated with GAD-Abs ( Blanc
et al., 2009; Malter et al., 2010; Markakis et al., 2014; Mata et al.,
2008). In particular, our data suggested that limbic encephalitis associ-
ated with intrathecal GAD-Abs was responsive to immunotherapy as
all patients achieved functional improvement after immunotherapy.
Previous studies also showed a favorable response to immunotherapy
with a parallel decrease in GAD-Ab titers ( Blanc et al., 2009; Markakis
et al., 2014). In contrast, a series of nine patients with GAD-associated
limbic encephalitis demonstrated inferior outcomes in seizure control
and memory function after corticosteroid therapy compared with
VGKC-Ab-positive patients ( Malter et al., 2010 ). Taken together with
the modest reduction in antibody titers, the unfavorable outcomes im-
plied that high-dose corticosteroids alone might be insufﬁcient for the
treatment of GAD-Ab-associated limbic encephalitis and that additional
immunotherapy might be required to more ef ﬁciently eliminate the

circulating antibodies. In agreement with this, all patients with limbic
encephalitis in our series received repeated rituximab infusions as the
2nd line immunotherapy before clinical improvement occurred.
Isolated epilepsy of temporal lobe origin was the second most
common syndrome (21.1%). Epilepsy was also present in patients
with limbic encephalitis or stiff-person syndrome, and most of them
had temporal lobe seizures. It has been increasingly accepted that
autoimmune mechanisms contributed in part to epilepsy even in the
absence of limbic encephalitis phenotypes, and GAD-Ab was one of
the best-known antibodies in immune-mediated epilepsy ( McKnight
et al., 2005; Quek et al., 2012 ). Previous data demonstrated that 3.9%
to 5.4% of patients with drug-resistant epilepsy had high serum titers
of GAD-Abs (
Lilleker et al., 2014; Peltola et al., 2000 ), and consistent
with our ﬁndings, most of the patients had temporal lobe epilepsy
(Errichiello et al., 2009; Falip et al., 2012; Liimatainen et al., 2010 ).
Although there were con ﬂicting results regarding immunotherapy
responses, the successful treatment of refractory epilepsy after immu-
notherapy has been reported in previous cases ( Farooqi et al., 2015;
Kanter et al., 2008 ). Furthermore, cortical GABA levels were reported
to decrease in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy and GAD-Abs,
but there was no difference in a composite measure of glutamate and
glutamine (Stagg et al., 2010). These ﬁndings supported the pathogenic
role of GAD-Abs in epilepsy, although the exact mechanism of GAD
autoimmunity has not been fully understood.
Cerebellar ataxia is a well-recognized neurological syndrome associ-
ated with GAD-Abs especially of high serum titers ( Honnorat et al.,
2001; Saiz et al., 2008 ). (Nanri et al., 2013 ) In our data, three patients
(15.8%) presented with subacute or chronic cerebellar ataxia, and
cerebellar dysfunction was corroborated by the brain imaging which
revealed marked cerebellar atrophy in one patient and cerebellar
hypometabolism in two. One patient who responded to immunothera-
py had relatively short disease duration (4 months) before therapy and
decreased glucose metabolism without apparent cerebellar atrophy.
These ﬁndings indicate that early immunotherapy might provide favor-
able outcomes in cerebellar ataxia associated with GAD-Abs, which is
consistent with previous study favoring the prompt immunotherapy
(Arino et al., 2014).
Notably, four patients with otherwise unclassi ﬁed syndromes
presented with isolated dizziness or diplopia. In a recent series of 34
patients with cerebellar ataxia and GAD-Abs, nine (26.5%) patients re-
ported episodes of diplopia or isolated vertigo without other evidence
of cerebellar dysfunction before ataxia was fully developed ( Arino
et al., 2014). These data indicated that subtle and transient symptoms
might herald the development of cerebellar ataxia. A long-term
follow-up study should be performed to con ﬁrm that non-speci ﬁc
symptoms, including dizziness, represent the early phase of GAD
autoimmunity and that earlier immunotherapy can help to prevent or
delay the development of obvious neurologic dysfunction.
In this study, we excluded the patients positive for serum GAD-Abs
from the analysis to focus on intrathecal-speci ﬁc GAD-Abs. Among 32
patients screened, however, 10 patients (31.3%) showed elevated
GAD-Abs in the paired serum samples. While two patients (#11 and

typically shown in GAD Ab-associated neurological syndromes, the
others revealed low-level Abs (1.02 –5.04 U/mL). Diagnostic values of
serum low-titer GAD-Abs have not been established mainly because
elevated GAD-Abs are also common in type 1 DM ( Saiz et al., 1997 ).
However, several studies reported that low-titer GAD-Abs were
implicated in cerebellar ataxia and epilepsy ( Errichiello et al., 2009;
Liimatainen et al., 2010; Nanri et al., 2013 ). Especially, Nanri et al.
(2013) demonstrated effectiveness of immunotherapy in patients
with cerebellar ataxia, providing the potential indications for immuno-
therapy in low-titer GAD-Abs.
Our study has limitations mostly regarding the measurement of
GAD-Abs in CSF. First, we used the commercial RIA kits which were orig-
inally developed for testing serum GAD-Abs. However, our RIA protocol
was not modiﬁed to make the CSF assays equivalent to those for serum,
and the methodological difference consequently might affect the anti-
body titers of CSF samples. Nevertheless, it does not alter the fact that
GAD-Abs are present in CSF tested, although the titers are too low to
emphasize their pathogenic relevance. Second, our ﬁndings were not
conﬁrmed by other methods to measure GAD-Abs. Immunohistochem-
istry is a commonly used method for analysis of GAD-Abs associated
with neurological syndromes, but it can only detect samples with high
GAD-Ab titers ( ≥ 2000 U/mL by RIA) and is not suitable for measure
low-titer antibodies ( Saiz et al., 2008 ). Further research using other
techniques such as immunoblots or cell-based assays will be helpful in
validating the presence of CSF-speciﬁc GAD-Abs. Finally, the study popu-
lation only included patients suspected to have autoimmune neurological
diseases, and lack of healthy controls hinders the understanding of clinical
utility and relevance of intrathecal GAD-Abs. Measuring CSF GAD-Abs in

5. Conclusions
Our study showed that intrathecal-speciﬁc antibodies to GAD were
found in patients with various neurological syndromes with a possible
autoimmune basis, such as limbic encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, crypto-
genic focal epilepsy, and stiff-person syndromes. However, measuring
GAD-Abs in CSF could not be used for diagnosis of GAD Ab-associated
neurological disorders because CSF GAD-Abs were also detected in
non-autoimmune neurological diseases. Intrathecal synthesis of
GAD-Abs at low titers may represent nonspeci ﬁc immune activation
and in ﬂammation within the CNS. Further investigations with other
laboratory techniques as well as different disease entities are needed
to con ﬁrm the presence of intrathecal-speci ﬁc GAD-Abs and their
clinical signiﬁcance.
